events.title: Trajan enters Rome on foot
events.summary: After more than a year on the Rhine and Danube following his accession, Trajan entered Rome in 99 on foot, embracing senators and greeting knights by name; his wife Plotina, climbing the Palatine steps, declared that she would leave the palace the same woman she entered it.
events.detail: Pliny's Panegyricus (22-24) describes the crowds on roofs and the emperor's accessibility. The staged modesty, contrasted with Domitian, set the tone of the "civil princeps" (civilis princeps) and Trajan's good relations with the Senate. He distributed a congiarium and paid soldiers only half the customary donative.

events.title: Pliny and Tacitus prosecute Marius Priscus
events.summary: In January 100, with Trajan presiding as consul, Pliny and Tacitus prosecuted Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa, for taking bribes to condemn and execute innocent men; the three-day trial ended in his relegation and the forfeiture of 700,000 sesterces.
events.detail: Pliny's letter (2.11) describes speaking for nearly five hours, with Trajan concerned for his voice, and Tacitus replying "very eloquently and with the grandeur that marks his speaking". Repetundae trials before the Senate were a recurring check on provincial governors; Pliny also took part in the cases against Caecilius Classicus (Baetica) and Julius Bassus (Bithynia).

events.title: Pliny's Panegyricus
events.summary: On 1 September 100 Pliny delivered his speech of thanks (gratiarum actio) for the suffect consulship before Trajan, later expanding it into the Panegyricus, the only Latin prose speech surviving from between Cicero and the fourth century.
events.detail: It contrasts Trajan, optimus princeps, with Domitian point by point: modesty, accessibility, liberty of the Senate, end of informers, sound finances. It became the model for the late antique Panegyrici Latini, in whose manuscript it heads the collection. Pliny's ten books of letters, published in stages c. 100-109, with Book 10 containing his correspondence with Trajan from Bithynia, are the other great source for the period.

events.title: Trajan's road and canal through the Iron Gates
events.summary: In 100 Trajan completed a road cut into the cliffs of the Danube gorge at the Iron Gates, partly carried on wooden cantilevers, and in 101 a canal at Sip (Sip) 3.2 km long to bypass the cataracts, preparing for the Dacian war.
events.detail: The Tabula Traiana inscription records that Trajan "cut through mountains and removed projections" to make the road; when the Djerdap dam raised the river in 1972 the plaque was moved 21 m higher. A second inscription found in 1969 records the canal built "because of the danger of the cataracts" to make the Danube navigable. Holes for the beams of the cantilevered road are still visible.
events.locName: Iron Gates gorge of the Danube (Tabula Traiana)

events.title: Markets of Trajan
events.summary: Built c. 100-110 in brick-faced concrete against the cut-back slope of the Quirinal behind Trajan's Forum, the so-called Markets of Trajan comprised a hemicycle and some 150 rooms on several levels around a vaulted hall and an ancient street, the Via Biberatica.
events.detail: Brick stamps date the construction to the early Trajanic years; the work is attributed to Apollodorus or his circle. The complex was probably not a market in the modern sense but a mixture of shops, offices (perhaps of the procurators of the Forum and the annona) and storage. Its great hall, roofed with six cross vaults, anticipates later bath and basilica design. It was converted into a fortified convent and the Torre delle Milizie in the Middle Ages and is now a museum.
events.debate: Function of the complex (market, offices or both) is debated.

events.title: Trajan's hexagonal harbour at Portus
events.summary: Around 100-112 Trajan added an inner hexagonal basin of 32 hectares to Claudius's silting harbour at Portus, with warehouses, a canal (Fossa Traiana) to the Tiber and a palatial complex, making it the main port of Rome for the grain fleets.
events.detail: Each side of the basin was 358 m long, giving some 2 km of quays; the basin survives as a lake in the Torlonia estate near Fiumicino airport. Recent excavations (Portus Project) have found a huge shipshed or arsenal and the Palazzo Imperiale. Portus gradually supplanted Ostia, which saw a building boom under Trajan and Hadrian. Trajan also built harbours at Centumcellae (Civitavecchia) and Ancona.

events.title: Bridge of Alcantara over the Tagus
events.summary: In 104-106 the architect Gaius Julius Lacer built for eleven municipia of Lusitania a granite bridge of six arches over the Tagus, 194 m long and nearly 50 m high, which he inscribed "pontem perpetui mansurum in saecula mundi".
events.detail: The inscriptions on the small temple at one end and on the triumphal arch at the centre name Trajan and the contributing towns. Its largest arches span almost 29 m. The bridge was broken in wars in 1214, 1760 and 1809 and repeatedly restored, and still carries traffic. Lacer was buried in the temple beside it.

events.title: Decebalus captures Pompeius Longinus
events.summary: At the start of the Second Dacian War in 105 Decebalus lured the Roman commander Gnaeus Pompeius Longinus to a parley and held him hostage, demanding the return of Dacian territory and war costs; Longinus took poison smuggled by a freedman so as not to be a bargaining counter.
events.detail: Dio tells the story. Decebalus had also sent deserters to assassinate Trajan in Moesia. Decebalus offered to return Longinus's body and ten captives in exchange for the freedman, whom Trajan refused to surrender. The episode shows the desperate final phase of Dacian resistance.

events.title: The treasure of Decebalus
events.summary: After the fall of Sarmizegetusa, Decebalus's companion Bicilis revealed where the king's treasure had been hidden: under the bed of the river Sargetia, which had been diverted by prisoners who were then killed. The plunder financed Trajan's building and games.
events.detail: John Lydus, quoting Trajan's physician Crito, gives figures of five million pounds of gold and ten million of silver, almost certainly inflated by a factor of ten or more, plus 500,000 prisoners. Even reduced, the booty funded the games of 107 (123 days with 11,000 animals and 10,000 gladiators), the Forum of Trajan, the baths, the alimenta and an upturn in coin output. Dacia's gold mines at Alburnus Maior (Rosia Montana) were exploited by Illyrian miners brought in after the conquest.
events.debate: Size of the booty: Crito's figures are generally reduced by Carcopino and others.

events.title: Colonia Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa founded
events.summary: Soon after the conquest, the first governor of Dacia, Decimus Terentius Scaurianus, founded the veteran colony of Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa some 40 km west of the destroyed Dacian capital, as the provincial capital.
events.detail: The foundation inscription names Scaurianus. The colony, laid out on the site of a legionary camp, had a forum, amphitheatre and the seat of the provincial council of the three Dacias. Eutropius (8.6) says Trajan brought "infinite numbers of people from the whole Roman world" to repopulate Dacia, though the scale of Dacian depopulation is disputed.

events.title: Trajan recalls worn coinage
events.summary: In 107 Trajan, according to Dio, melted down worn-out coins; the mint struck a series of "restoration" coins reproducing Republican denarii and earlier imperial aurei with the legend REST(ituit), while the denarius was slightly debased to about 89% silver.
events.detail: The restored types reproduce some 50 Republican moneyers' designs and earlier emperors from Caesar to Titus. Hoard evidence shows the disappearance of heavier pre-Neronian denarii from circulation after this date, supporting the idea of a deliberate recall. The Dacian booty may have made the operation possible.

events.title: Martyrdom of Ignatius of Antioch
events.summary: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was taken under guard to Rome to be thrown to the beasts under Trajan, c. 107-115, writing on the way seven letters to churches in Asia, Rome and to Polycarp of Smyrna.
events.detail: The letters are the earliest witness to a single bishop (monepiskopos) presiding over presbyters and deacons in each church, attack docetists who denied Christ's physical suffering and Judaising Christians, and use the term "catholic church" for the first time. His letter to the Romans begs them not to intervene: "I am God's wheat, ground by the teeth of wild beasts." The authenticity of the "middle recension" of seven letters, established by Lightfoot and Zahn, is still occasionally challenged.
events.debate: Date (often c. 110-117) and authenticity of the letters.

events.title: Plutarch writes the Parallel Lives
events.summary: In the reigns of Trajan and Hadrian, Plutarch of Chaeronea, priest of Apollo at Delphi, wrote 23 surviving pairs of Greek and Roman lives, dedicated to the consular Quintus Sosius Senecio, together with the enormous corpus of essays known as the Moralia.
events.detail: Plutarch was a Roman citizen (Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus) and, according to the Suda, received consular ornaments from Trajan and a procuratorship of Achaea from Hadrian, though these honours are doubted. He stressed that he wrote lives, not histories, revealing character in small things. Through Amyot's French and North's English translations the Lives became Shakespeare's main source for Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus.

events.title: Dedication of the Baths of Trajan
events.summary: On 22 June 109 Trajan opened his baths on the Oppian, designed by Apollodorus over the buried wings of Nero's Golden House, the first of the great symmetrical imperial thermae with a central bathing block set in a vast walled precinct with exedrae, libraries and gardens.
events.detail: The complex covered about 10 hectares, three times the Baths of Titus next door. The Fasti Ostienses give the date, two days before the opening of the Aqua Traiana. Its plan set the model for the Baths of Caracalla and Diocletian. Building over the Domus Aurea preserved its rooms, whose rediscovery around 1480 inspired Renaissance "grotesque" decoration.

events.title: Aqua Traiana opened
events.summary: On 24 June 109 Trajan opened the Aqua Traiana, bringing spring water some 57 km from around Lake Bracciano to the Janiculum and Trastevere, which had depended on the poor water of the Alsietina.
events.detail: Coins show a reclining river god in a grotto with the legend AQVA TRAIANA. The aqueduct drove mills on the Janiculum that ground the city's grain in late antiquity; when the Goths cut it in 537 Belisarius set up floating mills on the Tiber. Pope Paul V restored it as the Acqua Paola (1612). In 2009-2010 its source sanctuary (nymphaeum) was identified under a church near Manziana.

events.title: Tropaeum Traiani dedicated at Adamclisi
events.summary: In 109 Trajan dedicated to Mars Ultor a colossal circular victory monument at Adamclisi in the Dobrudja, 38 m in diameter and crowned with a trophy, near an altar listing some 3,800 Roman soldiers who died in the battle of 102.
events.detail: Its 54 metopes, carved in a vigorous provincial style, show Roman legionaries in segmented and mail armour fighting Dacians with the two-handed falx, Sarmatians and Germanic warriors; some legionaries wear greaves and arm guards, perhaps an adaptation to the falx. The town of Tropaeum Traiani grew beside it. The monument was reconstructed in concrete in 1977, with the originals in the site museum.

events.title: Via Nova Traiana from Bostra to the Red Sea
events.summary: Between 111 and 114 the governor Gaius Claudius Severus built the Via Nova Traiana across the new province of Arabia, 430 km from Bostra to Aila on the Gulf of Aqaba, "opened and paved from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea" in the words of its milestones.
events.detail: The road linked the legionary base of III Cyrenaica at Bostra with Philadelphia (Amman), Petra and the port of Aila, serving the incense and Red Sea trade as well as military movements; hundreds of milestones survive. Papyri from the Cave of Letters and the Babatha archive show the province's administration within a generation of annexation.

events.title: Arch of Trajan at Beneventum
events.summary: In 114 the Senate dedicated an arch to Trajan at Beneventum, where his new Via Traiana branched from the Appian Way towards Brundisium, its reliefs presenting the emperor's civil and military achievements, from the alimenta to the reception of eastern envoys.
events.detail: The arch is the best-preserved of its type, with panels facing the city on domestic themes (the Senate and Capitoline gods welcoming Trajan, the alimenta, veterans' settlements) and those facing the country on provincial ones (the Danube frontier, Mesopotamia). Some reliefs may have been completed under Hadrian, who appears prominently.

events.title: Trajan conquers northern Mesopotamia
events.summary: In 115 Trajan advanced from Armenia into northern Mesopotamia, received the submission of Abgar VII of Edessa, who won favour through his handsome son, and of other dynasts, and took Nisibis and Batnae, earning the title Parthicus; Lusius Quietus cleared the Mardi east of the Tigris.
events.detail: Dio says Trajan was hailed imperator several times and the Senate voted him the right to celebrate as many triumphs as he wished. Mannus, the Arab dynast, and Sporaces of Anthemusia submitted or were deposed. In winter 115/116 Trajan was at Antioch when the earthquake struck.

events.title: Trajan reaches the Persian Gulf
events.summary: After taking Ctesiphon in 116, Trajan sailed down the Tigris to Charax Spasinou, where the king of Characene, Athambelus, submitted; seeing a ship leaving for India, he said that he would have crossed to India too if he were younger, like Alexander, and later sacrificed at Babylon in the room where Alexander died.
events.detail: The Persian Gulf expedition was the farthest point of Roman conquest. A Latin inscription from the Farasan islands in the southern Red Sea shows Roman presence in the region under the Antonines. While Trajan was in the south, the newly conquered lands revolted behind him.
events.locName: Charax Spasinou, head of the Persian Gulf

events.title: Revolt of Mesopotamia against Trajan
events.summary: In 116, while Trajan was at the Gulf, the conquered territories rose: the general Maximus Santra was defeated and killed, and Seleucia and the Jewish communities of Mesopotamia revolted; Lusius Quietus retook and burned Nisibis and Edessa, Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander captured Seleucia, and Trajan crowned the Parthian prince Parthamaspates at Ctesiphon.
events.detail: Trajan then failed to take Hatra in 117, his army suffering from heat and flies, and fell ill. Quietus's brutal suppression of the Mesopotamian Jews led to his appointment as governor of Judaea. Hadrian abandoned Mesopotamia and Assyria on his accession, and Parthamaspates was soon driven out, becoming king of Osroene.

events.title: Lusius Quietus governs Judaea; the "War of Qitos"
events.summary: After suppressing the Jews of Mesopotamia, the Moorish general Lusius Quietus was made governor of Judaea in 117, the province being raised to consular rank; rabbinic sources remember a "war of Qitos" (polemos shel Qitos), and Marcius Turbo crushed the revolt in Egypt and Cyrene.
events.detail: The Mishnah (Sotah 9.14) lists decrees issued "in the war of Qitos" banning bridal crowns and the teaching of Greek. Hadrian recalled and then executed Quietus in 118 with three other consulars. Legio II Traiana may have been stationed in Judaea at this time, giving the province a second legion before the Bar Kokhba war.

events.title: Unrest in Britain at Hadrian's accession
events.summary: The Historia Augusta says that at Hadrian's accession "the Britons could not be kept under Roman control", and Fronto later compared the soldiers killed in Britain under Hadrian with the losses of the Jewish war; Quintus Pompeius Falco restored order c. 118-122 and coins of 119 show BRITANNIA.
events.detail: The crisis is connected in modern discussion with the disappearance of legio IX Hispana, last attested at York in 108, though the legion's fate is debated (transfer to the Rhine at Nijmegen and loss in the East later are favoured). The unrest was a background to the decision to build Hadrian's Wall from 122.

events.title: Roxolani crisis and Hadrian's reorganisation of Dacia
events.summary: In 117-119 the Iazyges and Roxolani attacked the lower Danube; Hadrian negotiated with the Roxolanian king, restoring his subsidy, while Marcius Turbo held a special command over Dacia and Pannonia Inferior. Dacia was then divided into Superior and Inferior, with Porolissensis added c. 123.
events.detail: Dio and Eutropius preserve a story that Hadrian considered giving up Dacia and was dissuaded by the presence of so many Roman colonists; he removed the superstructure of Trajan's Danube bridge to prevent its use by raiders. The Roxolanian king Rasparaganus later lived at Pola as a Roman citizen, Publius Aelius Rasparaganus.

events.title: Hadrian on the Rhine and the frontier palisade
events.summary: Setting out on his first great tour in 121, Hadrian inspected the Rhine armies, enforcing discipline, removing luxuries from the camps and living like a soldier, and ordered a continuous wooden palisade "like a wall" along the open stretches of frontier in Germany.
events.detail: The Historia Augusta describes stakes planted deep and fastened together; dendrochronology has dated felled timbers of the Upper German palisade to the winter of 119/120 and later, matching the account. Hadrian ate camp food (bacon, cheese, sour wine), marched 20 miles in full kit and examined arms and soldiers' ages personally.
events.locName: Mogontiacum and the Upper German frontier

events.title: Hadrian winters at Tarraco
events.summary: After Britain and southern Gaul, where he built a basilica at Nemausus in memory of Plotina, Hadrian wintered in 122/123 at Tarraco, restoring the temple of Augustus, convening an assembly of all Spain about army recruitment and escaping an attack by a slave with a sword, whom he handed over to doctors as insane.
events.detail: Hadrian never visited his ancestral town of Italica, though he gave it colonial status and lavish buildings. The Italicenses notoriously declined colonial status in favour of being a municipium, Hadrian's speech on which is preserved by Aulus Gellius. Recruitment resistance (the Italians mocked it as "Trebatian", the Spaniards objected strongly) suggests difficulty in filling the legions.

events.title: Hadrian averts a Parthian war on the Euphrates
events.summary: In 123, hearing of preparations for war by Osroes, Hadrian hurried from the West to the Euphrates and settled the matter in a personal meeting, promising later to return Osroes's daughter, captured by Trajan at Ctesiphon in 116.
events.detail: The Historia Augusta credits Hadrian with resolving the crisis by conversation alone. Hadrian sent the daughter back in 129 and promised the golden throne taken at Ctesiphon, which Antoninus Pius later refused to return. The episode shows Hadrian's policy of securing the frontier by diplomacy after abandoning Trajan's conquests.

events.title: Hadrian in Bithynia and Asia; Antinous
events.summary: Wintering in Bithynia in 123/124, Hadrian funded the rebuilding of Nicomedia and Nicaea after a severe earthquake; it was probably here that he met Antinous of Claudiopolis (Bithynium), who became his companion.
events.detail: Hadrian then toured the cities of Asia, founding Hadrianotherae where he had killed a bear, and Hadriani and Hadrianeia in Mysia. The cities competed for his benefactions, and the many places named Hadrianopolis or Hadriane date from these journeys. Antinous is first securely attested in Hadrian's company on the later journey of 128-130.

events.title: Hadrian initiated at Eleusis
events.summary: In autumn 124 Hadrian, wintering at Athens, was initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries, as Augustus had been, and in 125 presided over the Dionysia in Greek dress as archon; he gave Athens new laws, an oil law regulating exports and lavish gifts.
events.detail: He returned to Eleusis for the higher grade (epopteia) in 128. The Athenian oil law, preserved in an inscription, required producers to sell a third of their oil to the city. Hadrian's identification with Athens culminated in the completion of the Olympieion and the founding of the Panhellenion in 131-132.

events.title: Hadrian climbs Etna to see the sunrise
events.summary: On his way back to Rome in 125 Hadrian climbed Etna to watch the sunrise, which was said to appear in rainbow colours, and repeated the exploit on Mount Casius in Syria in 129, where a lightning bolt struck the victim and the attendant during his sacrifice.
events.detail: The Historia Augusta preserves both anecdotes. Hadrian's curiosity (curiositas) and love of travel, satirised by the poet Florus ("I don't want to be Caesar, wandering among the Britons ... enduring Scythian frosts"), to which Hadrian replied with a jibe about Florus haunting taverns, were key traits of his self-presentation.

events.title: Hadrian's second stay at Athens; pater patriae
events.summary: In 128, after accepting the title pater patriae and visiting Africa, Hadrian spent the winter of 128/129 at Athens with Sabina and Antinous, receiving the epopteia at Eleusis and planning the completion of the Olympieion.
events.detail: Coins from 128 call him P P and Sabina appears as Augusta with a new hairstyle. Hadrian's building in Athens included a new quarter (the "city of Hadrian" marked by his arch, inscribed on one side "This is Athens, the old city of Theseus" and on the other "This is the city of Hadrian and not of Theseus"), an aqueduct finished under Antoninus, a gymnasium and the great library.

events.title: Hadrian tours Asia, Cappadocia and Syria
events.summary: In 129 Hadrian passed through Caria, Cilicia and Cappadocia to Antioch, summoned the client kings of the East to a conference, climbed Mount Casius, and visited Palmyra, which took the name Hadriana Palmyra, and the cities of Arabia.
events.detail: At the conference the Iberian king Pharasmanes II refused to come, while others received gifts. Hadrian quarrelled with Antioch, planning to split Syria, and favoured Damascus and Tyre. A Palmyrene inscription honours the local notable Males Agrippa for hosting Hadrian and his army. Petra became Hadriane Petra.

events.title: Hadrian at Gerasa, Petra and Jerusalem
events.summary: In winter 129/130 and spring 130 Hadrian toured Arabia and Judaea, stayed at Gerasa, where a monumental arch was built for his visit, and on seeing the ruins of Jerusalem decided to refound it as the colony Aelia Capitolina.
events.detail: The triple Arch of Hadrian at Gerasa, dated 129/130, stands south of the city. Coins of 130-131 advertise his arrival (ADVENTVI AVG IVDAEAE). Whether the foundation of Aelia and the ban on circumcision provoked the Bar Kokhba revolt or followed it is one of the central debates of the period.
events.debate: Whether Aelia Capitolina was founded before (Dio) or after (Eusebius) the revolt.

events.title: Hadrian in Egypt: Pompey's tomb, the Museum and the lion hunt
events.summary: Arriving in Egypt in summer 130, Hadrian restored Pompey's tomb at Pelusium, debated with the scholars of the Museum at Alexandria, and hunted a man-eating lion in the Libyan desert with Antinous, an event celebrated in verse by Pancrates and in a hunting tondo later reused on the Arch of Constantine.
events.detail: A papyrus fragment of Pancrates' poem describes the lion's wounding and the red lotus said to have sprung from its blood, which was named after Antinous. Hadrian's questions to the professors and his mockery of their pretensions became anecdotes in the Historia Augusta. From Alexandria the imperial party sailed up the Nile in the autumn.

events.title: Foundation of Antinoopolis
events.summary: On 30 October 130, near the place where Antinous drowned in the Nile, Hadrian founded the Greek city of Antinoopolis, with settlers drawn from Ptolemais and the Fayum, privileges modelled on Naucratis, and a cult of the deified youth as Osiris-Antinous.
events.detail: Antinoites enjoyed exemption from liturgies elsewhere, the right to intermarry with Egyptians and an alimentary fund for their children. The city was laid out on a Hippodamian grid with a theatre, hippodrome and colonnaded streets; the Via Hadriana (137) linked it with Berenice on the Red Sea. The cult of Antinous spread across the Greek East with games, temples and some 2,000 statues and coins. The Obelisk of Antinous now on the Pincian probably stood at his tomb, possibly at Hadrian's Villa.

events.title: Hadrian and Sabina hear the Colossus of Memnon
events.summary: On 19-21 November 130 Hadrian and Sabina visited the northern Colossus of Memnon at Thebes, which "sang" at dawn; the court poet Julia Balbilla carved four Greek epigrams in Aeolic dialect on its leg recording that Memnon sang for the empress only on the second day and for Hadrian on the third.
events.detail: The statue, cracked by an earthquake in 27 BC, emitted a sound at sunrise, probably caused by heating and evaporation of dew in the fissures; it fell silent after Septimius Severus repaired it c. 199. Some 107 Greek and Latin inscriptions by Roman visitors, including prefects of Egypt, cover its legs.

sources.w: Les inscriptions grecques et latines du Colosse de Memnon (Bernand)

events.title: Arrian's Periplus of the Euxine
events.summary: Around 131-132 Arrian, governor of Cappadocia, sailed along the south-eastern Black Sea coast inspecting forts from Trapezus to Phasis and Sebastopolis (Dioscurias), and sent Hadrian a report in Greek, the Periplus Ponti Euxini, together with a Latin dispatch now lost.
events.detail: At Trapezus he found Hadrian's statue poorly made and asked for a better one; at Phasis he described the fort with its four hundred picked soldiers, artillery and ditches, and at Apsarus he paid five cohorts. He recorded the client kings of the Colchian peoples, appointed by Hadrian or Trajan. Arrian's other works include the Anabasis of Alexander, the Indike, the Tactica (136) and the Discourses of Epictetus.
events.locName: Phasis and the eastern Black Sea

events.title: Library of Hadrian at Athens
events.summary: Hadrian built at Athens a vast colonnaded enclosure of 122 by 82 m with a hundred columns of Phrygian marble, pools, a library hall and lecture rooms, dedicated c. 132 during his last visit, which Pausanias lists among his gifts to the city.
events.detail: The east side contained the book rooms with niches for scrolls, flanked by reading halls. Damaged in the Herulian sack of 267 and restored c. 410, it later contained a tetraconch church and then the Byzantine Megali Panagia. Its west facade with Corinthian columns still stands on Areos Street.
events.locName: Athens, north of the Roman Agora

events.title: Letters of Bar Kokhba and the Babatha archive
events.summary: Caves in the Judaean desert explored in 1951-1961 yielded letters in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek from Shimon bar Kosiba, "prince of Israel", to his commanders at Ein Gedi, and the legal archive of Babatha, a Jewish woman of Mahoza in Arabia, whose family fled there in 132-135.
events.detail: The letters show Bar Kosiba demanding the gathering of the four species for Sukkot, threatening officers who neglect orders, and administering land leases dated by "year of the redemption of Israel". The Babatha papers (35 documents, 94-132) illustrate marriage contracts, guardianship, property disputes and Roman provincial courts in Arabia. Skeletons in the Cave of Letters attest the refugees' fate.
events.locName: Nahal Hever and Wadi Murabba'at, Judaean desert

events.title: Hadrianic decrees and the aftermath of the Bar Kokhba war
events.summary: After the revolt Jews were banned from entering Aelia Capitolina except, later, on the 9th of Av, and rabbinic tradition remembers decrees forbidding circumcision, Sabbath observance and public teaching of the Torah, with the execution of sages such as Akiva (the "Ten Martyrs").
events.detail: Dio says 580,000 men were killed and 985 villages destroyed, figures probably exaggerated but reflecting the devastation of Judaea, after which the Jewish centre shifted to Galilee. Antoninus Pius allowed Jews to circumcise their own sons (Modestinus, Digest 48.8.11). The extent and duration of the "persecution" (shmad) is debated.
events.debate: Whether the circumcision ban caused the revolt or was a punishment for it.

events.title: Pons Aelius built
events.summary: In 134 Hadrian built the Pons Aelius across the Tiber as a monumental approach to his mausoleum, with three main arches and ramps at either end.
events.detail: The dedication inscription, recorded in the Middle Ages, dates it to Hadrian's 18th tribunician year. The bridge survives as the Ponte Sant'Angelo; Bernini's workshop added the ten angels with the instruments of the Passion in 1669-1671. In 1450 a crowd of jubilee pilgrims crushed on it caused the collapse of its parapets.

events.title: Mausoleum of Hadrian
events.summary: Hadrian's dynastic tomb on the right bank of the Tiber, begun c. 130 and completed by Antoninus Pius in 139, was a cylindrical drum 64 m across on a square base, crowned with a mound and a bronze quadriga, which received the ashes of emperors down to Caracalla.
events.detail: A spiral ramp led to the central burial chamber. Hadrian, Sabina and Lucius Aelius were among the first interred; the inscriptions of the burials were recorded before they were lost. Incorporated in the Aurelian Wall, it became a fortress; its defenders hurled statues on the Goths in 537. The name Castel Sant'Angelo derives from Gregory the Great's vision of the archangel Michael ending a plague in 590.

events.title: Hadrian's legal and administrative reforms
events.summary: Besides the codified edict, Hadrian forbade masters to kill slaves without a magistrate's sentence, to sell slaves to gladiatorial trainers or brothel-keepers without cause, or to castrate them; abolished private prisons (ergastula); appointed four consulars as judges for Italy; and gave the agreed opinions of licensed jurists the force of law.
events.detail: He also restricted the Silanian torture of slaves to those near enough to have heard, placed equestrians rather than freedmen in the palace secretariats, created the advocatus fisci, and gave his council (consilium) of jurists a formal role. The SC Tertullianum, passed under Hadrian, gave a mother with the ius liberorum the right to inherit from her children. The Italian consulars were abolished by Antoninus and revived as iuridici by Marcus.

events.title: Lex Hadriana de rudibus agris
events.summary: Inscriptions from the imperial estates of the Bagradas valley (Ain el-Djemala, Ain Wassel) record a "Hadrianic law on uncultivated lands" allowing tenants to occupy waste or neglected land and plant olives and vines, with rent-free periods (ten years for olives, five for fruit trees) and hereditary rights of possession.
events.detail: The law extended the earlier Lex Manciana (known from Henchir Mettich, 116/117), under which coloni paid a third of their crops to the estate. The Souk el-Khmis inscription of 180-183 records tenants of the saltus Burunitanus appealing to Commodus against excessive labour demands by the contractor. The texts show the expansion of olive culture that made Africa the empire's oil producer.

events.title: Mining regulations of Vipasca
events.summary: Two bronze tablets found at Aljustrel in 1876 and 1906 preserve regulations for the imperial copper and silver mining district of Vipasca under Hadrian, setting out the rights of lessees of mine shafts and the monopolies in the mining village (baths, cobbling, barbering, auctioneering).
events.detail: The procurator of the mines sold the right to work a shaft; the lessee had to begin work within 25 days and pay half the ore to the fiscus. Rules governed drainage galleries, timber supports and the sale of shares. The baths had to be heated daily and open for women from dawn to the seventh hour and men in the afternoon, and teachers were exempt from taxes.

events.title: Plotina's petition for the Epicurean school at Athens
events.summary: In 121 the widowed Plotina petitioned Hadrian to allow the head of the Epicurean school at Athens to choose his successor from among non-citizens and to make his choice by will in Greek; Hadrian agreed, and her letter to the Epicureans calling him "benefactor and overseer of all culture" survives on stone.
events.detail: The inscription (IG II2 1099) shows an empress acting as patron of a philosophical school and her personal adherence to Epicureanism. Marcus Aurelius later endowed chairs for all four major schools at Athens in 176.

events.title: Suetonius's Lives of the Caesars and his dismissal
events.summary: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, Hadrian's secretary for correspondence (ab epistulis), dedicated the Lives of the Twelve Caesars to the praetorian prefect Septicius Clarus c. 121, and in 122 both were dismissed for behaving too familiarly towards the empress Sabina.
events.detail: An inscription from Hippo Regius records his career: in charge of the imperial libraries, of studies (a studiis) and of correspondence. His access to the palace archives shows in quotations from Augustus's letters in the early lives; the later lives are thinner, perhaps after he lost access. The thematic arrangement (family, career, public acts, private habits, death) and gossip made it the model for imperial biography from the Historia Augusta to Einhard.

events.title: Juvenal's Satires
events.summary: Decimus Junius Juvenalis published sixteen verse satires in five books between about 110 and 130, indignant portraits of Rome's vices: the dangers of city life (3), Domitian's turbot council (4), women (6), the vanity of human wishes (10).
events.detail: Book 1 refers to the trial of Marius Priscus (100); Satire 7 opens with hope in a new Caesar, probably Hadrian; Satire 15 mentions a consul of 127. Juvenal gave the world "panem et circenses" (10.81), "mens sana in corpore sano" (10.356) and "quis custodiet ipsos custodes?" (6.347-348, in the Oxford fragment). Almost nothing reliable is known of his life; a late tradition says he was exiled to Egypt in old age.

events.title: The Tariff of Palmyra
events.summary: In April 137 the council of Palmyra inscribed in Greek and Palmyrene a revised tax law, one of the longest inscriptions of the Roman East, listing dues on slaves, dry goods, purple wool, perfumes, olive oil, salted fish, animals and prostitutes, with earlier rulings by Roman governors such as Germanicus and Mucianus.
events.detail: The tariff shows that taxes on goods consumed in the city were set locally but under Roman supervision, and preserves the rule that salt was to be measured in the Roman way. The stone, 5 m wide, was taken to St Petersburg in 1901 by Prince Abamelek-Lazarev and is in the Hermitage.
